The logistic regression is a predictive model trained on historical data. It accurately identifies that inactivity (days_since_last_active) is strongly associated with churn — that's useful for prioritising who to target. But a predictive association does not mean that sending these users a re-engagement email will close the 38 − 9 = 29 percentage point gap.

To make that causal claim, we need to know: among users who were inactive for 15+ days, does receiving the campaign cause fewer of them to churn? The historical model cannot answer this — it was built on users who were left to churn or retain on their own, without the campaign. The counterfactual (what would have happened to targeted users without the campaign) is unobservable from the observational regression.

Additionally, there may be confounders: inactive users may be disproportionately on trial plans, may have started during a seasonal period, or may have already found a competitor. Targeting them without understanding why they're inactive may produce low conversion rates even if the campaign is impactful in principle.

The appropriate next step is an A/B experiment: randomly assign some at-risk users to receive the campaign and others to a holdout, then compare churn rates.

Option A conflates predictive accuracy with treatment effect — the 38% vs. 9% difference is the model's estimate of the conditional churn probability, not an estimate of the campaign effect (which requires a randomised comparison).

Option C: statistical significance (p < 0.001) means the coefficient is estimated with high precision in the historical sample. It says nothing about causal or practical impact.

Option D: the choice between logistic regression and survival analysis affects the functional form and handling of censoring, not whether the coefficient is causally identifiable.
hints: A regression trained on historical data tells you who churned. Does it tell you what would happen if you intervened on them?
What would you need to measure to know whether the campaign actually reduces churn, rather than just predicting who is at risk?

title: Post-Experiment Threshold Change
description:
The team runs the re-engagement campaign as an A/B test (50/50 split, 20,000 users per arm, 60-day measurement window). Results: treatment arm 18% churn vs. control arm 22% churn (absolute reduction: 4 pp, p = 0.03, pre-registered primary metric).

The PM then requests a subgroup analysis by inactivity threshold:
- 15–19 days inactive: 3% churn reduction (p = 0.18)
- 20+ days inactive: 6% churn reduction (p = 0.01)

The PM says: 'The 20+ day cutoff works better. Let's change the targeting rule to 20 days and use the 6pp reduction as our headline metric.'

What is the correct statistical concern with adopting the 20-day threshold as the new rule?
options: The subgroup analysis is valid because users inactive 20+ days had the stronger effect; changing the threshold to match the largest observed effect is standard adaptive experimentation practice

Selecting the threshold post-hoc based on whichever subgroup showed the largest effect is a form of p-hacking (HARKing): the 20-day result was not pre-registered, and searching across two possible thresholds doubles the chance of finding a spuriously significant result. The 6pp / p=0.01 result should be treated as a hypothesis-generating finding requiring a new pre-registered experiment at the 20-day cutoff
The issue is purely practical: 20+ days has fewer users than 15+ days, so the campaign reaches fewer people, which reduces total retained users even if the per-user effect is larger
There is no concern — the overall experiment was pre-registered, so any subgroup analysis from that experiment inherits its validity
explanation:
Option B correctly identifies the HARKing (Hypothesising After Results are Known) / multiple comparisons problem.

Pre-registration binds the inferential logic to a specific primary metric and analysis plan. When you search across multiple possible thresholds and select the one with the best result, you are performing an implicit multiple comparison — even if you only selected two thresholds. With two comparisons at α = 0.05, the family-wise error rate rises to approximately 1 − (0.95)² ≈ 10%. The p = 0.01 result at the 20-day cutoff, found through post-hoc searching, does not carry the usual 5% Type I error guarantee.

The correct treatment: use the pre-registered 15-day result (p = 0.03, 4pp reduction) as the causal finding. Treat the 20-day subgroup as a hypothesis for a NEW experiment — pre-register 'we expect the 20-day threshold to show a 5–6pp reduction' and run a clean test.

This distinction matters in production: teams that routinely post-hoc select the 'best-looking' threshold calibrate themselves to be wrong far more than 5% of the time, eroding statistical discipline across the org.

Option A describes exploratory adaptive experimentation, but that framework requires upfront registration of the adaptive stopping rules — it is not a license for post-hoc selection.

Option C is a valid practical consideration about campaign reach, but it does not address the statistical problem with the threshold change. The core issue is the inferential claim, not the targeting scale.

Option D is wrong: pre-registration of the overall experiment does not validate post-hoc subgroup selection as a causal finding. Subgroup results can always be generated by random variation in subgroup assignment; their statistical credibility depends on whether they were specified in advance.
hints: How many candidate thresholds did the team actually evaluate (even implicitly)? How does that affect the chance of finding a p < 0.05 result by random variation?
What is the difference between 'this subgroup analysis is confirmatory' and 'this subgroup analysis is exploratory'? Which is this?

title: Campaign Effect Shrinks 3× at Scale
description:
The 15-day re-engagement campaign was validated in a 20,000-user A/B test (4 pp churn reduction, p = 0.03). The team rolls out the campaign to all 1 million eligible users. After 60 days, the team compares the rollout cohort against a historical baseline and observes only a 1.3 pp churn reduction — roughly one-third of the pilot effect.

The PM asks: 'Did our experiment mislead us, or is something else happening?'

Which combination of factors best explains why a validated pilot effect often shrinks at full scale?
options: The experiment misled you: the p-value of 0.03 means there was a 3% chance the result was a false positive, and at scale the false positive materialised

Heterogeneous treatment effects and operational degradation together: the pilot naturally included the most responsive subpopulation (users who had recently gone inactive for the first time and are genuinely reactivatable), while full-scale rollout includes users who are chronically inactive or churned for other reasons. Additionally, campaign quality (personalisation, timing) often degrades when volume increases 50×

The historical baseline comparison is always valid for measuring campaign effects at scale; the 1.3pp figure should be treated as the true treatment effect, and the pilot A/B test was the misleading one
The shrinkage is due to seasonality alone; running the pilot and the rollout in different months always produces this artifact
explanation:
Option B identifies the two most common mechanisms for pilot-to-production shrinkage in product experiments.

**Heterogeneous treatment effects (HTE):** The pilot ran on a 20,000-user sample that, unless specifically stratified to represent the full eligible population, likely overrepresented the users most likely to respond (e.g., users who recently crossed the 15-day threshold for the first time, who may be experiencing temporary disengagement). When the campaign scales to ALL 1 million eligible users — including chronically inactive users, users who have already churned in spirit, or users from acquisition cohorts with structurally lower retention — the average treatment effect is pulled down by the less-responsive subpopulations.

**Operational degradation:** Personalised re-engagement campaigns are often more thoughtfully executed at pilot scale (better subject lines, tighter timing, closer monitoring). At 50× volume, execution quality often decays — emails arrive at suboptimal times, personalisation logic hits edge cases, and the novelty effect wears off as more users receive them simultaneously.

**Historical baseline bias (Option C's problem):** Comparing rollout users to a historical baseline introduces confounding from time trends (seasonal effects, product changes, competitive dynamics). A historical baseline is not a valid control group — only a concurrent randomised holdout is. The 1.3pp figure from the historical comparison may under- or overstate the true effect.

Option A misinterprets the p-value: p = 0.03 means that IF the null hypothesis were true (no effect), we would observe a result this extreme about 3% of the time. It does NOT mean there is a 3% chance the result is a false positive — that depends on the prior probability of an effect existing (base rate), not just p.

Option D is a plausible nuisance factor (seasonality) but is incomplete; it explains some of the discrepancy through the historical baseline problem (Option C's issue) rather than explaining the HTE and operational degradation that are the primary drivers of pilot-to-production shrinkage.
hints: Who are the 20,000 users in the pilot versus the 1,000,000 at scale? Are they the same mix of responsiveness?
Comparing the rollout to a historical baseline is not the same as a concurrent A/B test. Why does that matter for the 1.3pp estimate?

title: Simpson's Paradox in Feature Adoption
description:
A product team evaluates whether Feature F increases purchase conversion:

| Group | With Feature F | Without Feature F |
|---|---|---|
| Overall | 8.0% conversion | 12.0% conversion |
| Power users | 20.0% | 15.0% |
| Casual users | 5.0% | 4.0% |

In every user segment, Feature F is associated with higher conversion. Yet in the overall population, Feature F is associated with lower conversion (8% vs. 12%).

What is the correct explanation, and what should the PM do?
options: The data is internally inconsistent; numbers that show a reversal across groups and overall cannot both be correct and should be re-pulled

Simpson's Paradox: the overall reversal is caused by a confounding variable (user type) that is correlated with both Feature F adoption and conversion. Because casual users dominate the Feature F group (lower baseline conversion) and power users dominate the non-Feature-F group (higher baseline conversion), the aggregate comparison is confounded by user type. The correct within-segment results show F is beneficial; the PM should report segment-level results and consider user type as a covariate in any further analysis
Feature F has a negative overall effect that somehow disappears in segments; this is a sign of a measurement error in the segment data
The overall result (8% vs. 12%) is the correct causal estimate because it uses the full sample; segment-level analyses always introduce bias by splitting the data
explanation:
Option B correctly identifies Simpson's Paradox.

Simpson's Paradox occurs when a trend present in every subgroup reverses or disappears when the subgroups are combined. Here, Feature F is associated with higher conversion in both power users (+5pp) and casual users (+1pp). But in the aggregate, F looks worse (−4pp). Why? Because Feature F adoption is skewed: most Feature F users are casual users (who have low baseline conversion), and most non-Feature-F users are power users (who have high baseline conversion). When groups are aggregated without controlling for user type, the conversion comparison conflates Feature F adoption with user type — a classic confounding problem.

The causal interpretation depends on the question: if the PM wants to know 'does F help a given user?', the within-segment results are the right answer (yes, it helps both types). If the PM wants to know 'did rolling out F to the actual adoption mix improve overall conversion?', the aggregate result reflects the real-world outcome but is dominated by the user-type composition effect, not the treatment effect of F itself.

For A/B test design, the right approach is to randomise Feature F assignment within each user type (stratified randomisation), which would show the causal per-type lift without the composition confound.

Option A is wrong: the numbers are mathematically consistent. A weighted average can move opposite to each component if the weights differ enough across groups. This is not a data error.

Option C is wrong for the same reason — the paradox is not evidence of measurement error; it has a precise mathematical explanation.

Option D is wrong: segment-level analysis is not inherently biased. When user type is a confounder, ignoring it in the aggregate analysis IS the bias.
hints: What fraction of Feature F users are power users versus casual users? What about the non-Feature-F group? Could the mix of user types explain the aggregate reversal?
A weighted average can move in the opposite direction to all its components if the weights differ between the two groups being compared. Is that what's happening here?

title: Pearson Correlation Coefficient
description: Implement `solve(xs, ys)` that computes the Pearson correlation coefficient between two equal-length lists of floats. Return a float. Raise `ValueError` if the lists have different lengths or if either list has zero variance (correlation is undefined).
solution_code:
def solve(xs: list[float], ys: list[float]) -> float:
    import math
    # Pearson r = cov(X,Y) / (std(X) * std(Y))
    # Equivalently: sum of (xi - x_bar)(yi - y_bar) / sqrt(SS_x * SS_y)
    if len(xs) != len(ys):
        raise ValueError('Lists must have equal length')
    n = len(xs)
    mean_x = sum(xs) / n
    mean_y = sum(ys) / n
    cov = sum((xi - mean_x) * (yi - mean_y) for xi, yi in zip(xs, ys))
    var_x = sum((xi - mean_x) ** 2 for xi in xs)
    var_y = sum((yi - mean_y) ** 2 for yi in ys)
    if var_x == 0 or var_y == 0:
        raise ValueError('Correlation undefined: zero variance in one or both variables')
    return cov / math.sqrt(var_x * var_y)
explanation: Pearson r = cov(X,Y) / (σ_X · σ_Y) = Σ(xi−x̄)(yi−ȳ) / √[Σ(xi−x̄)² · Σ(yi−ȳ)²]. The numerator is the sum of cross-deviations; the denominator normalises by both spreads. r ∈ [−1, 1]: 1 = perfect positive linear relationship, 0 = no linear relationship, −1 = perfect negative. Undefined when either variable has zero variance (a constant cannot correlate).
hints: Pearson r = sum of (xi−x̄)(yi−ȳ) in the numerator, divided by the product of the two root-sum-of-squares in the denominator.
The denominator is sqrt(SS_x * SS_y) where SS_x = sum of squared deviations from the mean.

title: CUPED: Does It Change the Point Estimate?
description:
A product team is designing an A/B test for a new onboarding flow. Primary metric: day-7 retention. A data scientist recommends using CUPED (Controlled-experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data), applying the 30-day pre-experiment day-7 retention rate as the covariate.

The PM asks: 'What does CUPED actually do? Does it change which treatment is better, or are we just tweaking statistics?'
options: CUPED adjusts the point estimate by removing covariate effects; it may change which variant appears better and is required for valid A/B test conclusions

CUPED reduces variance in the outcome metric by removing variance explained by the pre-experiment covariate, narrowing confidence intervals without (in expectation) changing the point estimate. The same experiment achieves higher power or requires smaller sample size
CUPED is a significance threshold adjustment similar to Bonferroni correction; it lowers the α level to account for the covariate
CUPED is only applicable when the pre-experiment and in-experiment periods use exactly the same metric definition; if they differ even slightly the method is invalid
explanation:
Option B is correct. CUPED subtracts a linear adjustment (θ × (covariate − E[covariate])) from the observed outcome, where θ is estimated by regressing the outcome on the covariate in the pre-experiment period. Because the covariate (pre-experiment retention) is independent of treatment assignment (since it was measured before randomisation), this adjustment removes covariate-driven noise from the metric without introducing bias into the treatment effect estimate. In expectation, the CUPED-adjusted mean difference equals the unadjusted mean difference — only the variance changes.

The benefit: narrower confidence intervals at the same sample size means either (a) the same experiment has higher power (more likely to detect a real effect), or (b) the same power can be achieved with fewer users or a shorter experiment window. For typical pre-experiment/in-experiment correlations in retention metrics (r ≈ 0.3–0.6), CUPED can reduce required sample size by 10–40%.

Option A describes a different technique (regression adjustment that can change point estimates when the covariate is correlated with unequal group sizes). CUPED specifically preserves the unbiased estimator.

Option C confuses CUPED with multiple-testing corrections; they are unrelated.

Option D is too restrictive; CUPED can be applied when the pre-experiment metric is a proxy for the in-experiment metric, not just an exact match. The key requirement is that the covariate was measured before randomisation and is correlated with the outcome.
hints: If CUPED subtracts a term that is independent of treatment assignment, what does that do to the expected value of the treatment effect estimate?
Variance reduction ≠ bias introduction. Think about what happens to the width of the confidence interval when you remove noise correlated with the outcome.

title: Switching the Primary Metric After Seeing a Near-Miss p-Value
description:
The onboarding A/B test concludes. Day-7 retention (pre-registered primary metric): +2.1pp, p = 0.07.

Before unblinding, the PM had seen a competitor's case study using day-14 retention as the primary metric. After unblinding, the PM says: 'Our day-7 missed significance. Let's re-run the analysis with day-14 retention as the primary metric — it's a better business measure anyway.'

What is the correct response?
options: Switching to day-14 retention is acceptable because it was motivated by a legitimate business reason (competitor best practice) identified before the experiment started

Switching the primary metric after observing the outcome violates the pre-registration contract. Regardless of the business rationale, choosing the metric whose result is more favorable after unblinding is HARKing (Hypothesising After Results are Known) and inflates the true Type I error rate. Day-7 retention p = 0.07 is the valid answer: the experiment did not meet its pre-specified threshold
p = 0.07 is close enough to 0.05 that the PM should ship the feature; the exact metric choice is a detail
Pre-registration is only required for academic research; in product experimentation you may freely change the primary metric as long as the sample size does not change
explanation:
Option B is correct. Pre-registration serves a specific statistical function: it fixes the inferential target before the data is observed, ensuring that the stated α (usually 5%) is the actual probability of a Type I error. When you observe a near-miss (p = 0.07) and then switch to a different metric — even with a plausible business justification — you are implicitly performing multiple comparisons. The switching is motivated by the outcome (looking for a metric that gives p < 0.05), which inflates the effective α beyond the nominal level.

The timing of the competitor case study is irrelevant: the PM saw it before the experiment but raised it after unblinding. What matters is that the metric switch was proposed AFTER observing the result. If day-14 retention were genuinely the right primary metric, it should have been pre-registered before the experiment started.

The correct path forward is one of: (a) accept the p = 0.07 result as a non-significant finding (the pre-registered threshold was not met), (b) treat day-14 retention as a hypothesis-generating finding requiring a new pre-registered experiment, or (c) discuss pre-specifying a composite metric for future experiments — after the current experiment is closed.

Option A illustrates a common rationalisation: 'legitimate business reason' does not rescue post-hoc metric selection. The statistical validity depends on when the decision was made relative to observing the data.

Option C promotes a threshold culture that the statistics do not support. p = 0.07 means: if the null is true, a result this extreme would occur 7% of the time. With a 5% threshold, it is a non-finding.

Option D is wrong: pre-registration is not just for academia. In industry, HARKing erodes the signal value of experimentation across the org — teams optimise to find a metric that clears the bar rather than measuring the actual intervention effect.
hints: When did the PM propose switching the metric — before or after seeing the result? Why does timing matter?
If you run 10 experiments and pick the metric that clears p < 0.05 for each one, what is the effective false positive rate across experiments?

title: Borderline p-Value + Unregistered Revenue Signal
description:
The onboarding experiment results are being reviewed:
- Day-7 retention (pre-registered primary): +2.1pp, p = 0.07
- Day-14 retention (secondary, pre-registered): +1.0pp, p = 0.31
- Revenue per user (not pre-registered): +$0.80, p = 0.04

PM: 'p = 0.07 is basically significant, and revenue went up — we should ship.'
Data scientist: 'The primary metric missed. We should not ship.'

Whose position is better supported?
options: The PM is right: a p-value just above 0.05 combined with a positive revenue signal provides overwhelming evidence. Strict adherence to pre-registered thresholds is an academic nicety, not a product necessity

The data scientist is more correct. The pre-registered metric missed the threshold (p = 0.07 > 0.05). The revenue signal was not pre-registered and constitutes an additional look — effectively searching for significance among multiple metrics after the primary failed, which inflates the family-wise Type I error. The experiment is a non-significant result on its stated primary outcome
Both are equally valid; the decision should be made by the senior PM based on business judgment

The data scientist is too strict: because the revenue metric is independent of the retention metric, it provides a fully independent causal estimate and its p = 0.04 is not affected by multiple testing concerns
explanation:
Option B is the correct statistical position, though real-world shipping decisions involve additional judgment.

The pre-registered primary metric (day-7 retention) missed its threshold. This is the answer the experiment was designed to give. The revenue metric, because it was not pre-registered, is subject to multiple-comparison inflation: with one pre-registered metric plus one ad hoc metric, the effective family-wise error rate is approximately 1 − (0.95)² ≈ 10%, not 5%. The p = 0.04 revenue result is consistent with random variation at that inflated rate.

Option A conflates 'directionally positive' with 'statistically valid.' The whole point of pre-registration is to bind the inference to a specific question before the data answers it. 'Basically significant' is not a well-defined statistical concept, and invoking it erodes the statistical rigour the pre-registration was designed to provide.

Option D is a common misunderstanding: independence between metrics does not remove the multiple-testing problem. When you look at N metrics and report any that hit p < 0.05, the Type I error rate scales with N regardless of whether the metrics are correlated with each other. Multiple testing correction depends on the number of tests, not their correlation structure (though the correction can be less conservative when tests are correlated).

Practically: a borderline primary + a positive unregistered secondary is a legitimate hypothesis for a follow-up experiment — with both metrics pre-registered. It is not grounds to ship from the current experiment.
hints: The revenue metric was not pre-registered. If you look at three metrics and any p < 0.05 gets flagged, what is the actual false positive rate?
What is the purpose of pre-registering a primary metric before the experiment runs? What statistical guarantee does it give?

title: SUTVA Violation in a Social Marketplace
description:
A marketplace (think: Etsy) tests a new product recommendation algorithm by randomly assigning 50% of buyers to see recommendations (treatment) and 50% to see the default browse experience (control).

Buyers in the treatment group click through to sellers' item pages at a higher rate. Some of those buyers share item links with friends via message or social media. Some of the friends receiving links are assigned to the control group.

A data scientist flags that this violates an important assumption. What assumption is violated, and what is the consequence for the experiment?
options: Randomisation balance: the sharing behavior means the treatment and control groups are no longer equal in size, invalidating the random assignment

SUTVA (Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption): SUTVA requires that a unit's outcome depends only on that unit's treatment assignment, not on other units' assignments. Here, control users receive item links generated by the treatment algorithm through social sharing — a direct interference between treated and control units. This inflates apparent control-group engagement, compressing the measured treatment effect (the treatment effect is underestimated)
The Central Limit Theorem no longer applies when social sharing exists, so hypothesis tests using normal approximations are invalid
SUTVA only applies to physical experiments; digital product experiments are not subject to spillover concerns because online behavior is individually tracked
explanation:
Option B correctly identifies the SUTVA violation.

SUTVA is one of the core assumptions of the potential outcomes framework for causal inference. It states: the potential outcome for unit i under treatment t depends only on unit i's assignment, not on the assignments of other units. When control users receive socially-shared links generated by the treatment algorithm, their engagement is partially influenced by treatment-arm behavior — a direct SUTVA violation.

The consequence here is attenuation bias on the treatment effect: the control group experiences some of the treatment's benefits indirectly (via shared links), making them more engaged than they would be in a world without the treatment. The measured gap between treatment and control understates the true treatment effect.

In severe cases — e.g., viral social products, marketplace supply-demand spillovers, or pricing experiments — SUTVA violations can even reverse the sign of the measured effect.

Common solutions include: geo-based randomisation (treatment and control assigned to non-overlapping geographic markets), time-based switchback designs (alternating treatment/control periods), or network-cluster randomisation (assigning connected users to the same arm).

Option A is wrong: random assignment is still valid (50/50 split), and unequal group sizes are not the issue here (the groups remain equal in assignment; it is the interference that is the problem).

Option C is wrong: the CLT is not threatened by sharing behavior; it is a property of sampling distributions regardless of within-sample interactions.

Option D is a misconception: SUTVA violations are particularly common and important in digital experiments precisely because digital products facilitate rapid user-to-user interactions, viral loops, and network effects.
hints: What does SUTVA require about the relationship between one unit's outcome and other units' treatment assignments?
If a control user clicks on a link shared from the treatment arm, does their outcome still reflect 'pure control' conditions?

title: Novelty Effect: Week 1 Engagement Spike That Dissipates
description:
A new interface design is A/B tested. Results by week:

| Week | Treatment engagement | Control engagement | Lift |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 68% | 52% | +16pp |
| 2 | 61% | 53% | +8pp |
| 3 | 56% | 53% | +3pp |
| 4 | 54% | 54% | 0pp |

The PM sees the week-1 result and says: 'We have a 16pp improvement — ship it.' The data scientist argues the experiment should run longer.

Which interpretation best describes what the data shows, and what should the team do?
options: The 16pp lift is the true treatment effect; later weeks are contaminated by control users learning about the new design, which suppresses the week-4 comparison

The data shows a classic novelty effect: users explore and engage more with any changed interface in the early period (treatment is 'new'), but engagement returns to baseline as the novelty wears off. The true steady-state effect appears to be near zero. Shipping based on week-1 data would overestimate the lasting value of the change; the experiment should run until engagement stabilizes
The experiment is invalid because the lift declined monotonically; a well-designed A/B test should show stable effects across all weeks
Novelty effects are only relevant for physical product experiments; digital interface changes do not exhibit novelty effects because users adapt instantly
explanation:
Option B correctly identifies a novelty effect and its implication.

A novelty effect occurs when the act of change itself — not the value of the change — drives the initial engagement lift. Users naturally pay more attention to anything new; this extra attention produces higher engagement in the first days or weeks. As users habituate to the new interface, engagement reverts toward the baseline. In this experiment, the lift dropped from 16pp → 8pp → 3pp → 0pp over four weeks, which is the pattern of a decaying novelty effect rather than a durable treatment benefit.

The practical implication is significant: if the PM ships based on week-1 data, they will expect a 16pp sustained improvement and be disappointed (and confounded about why it disappeared). The correct approach is to run the experiment until the treatment-control delta stabilises — typically 2–4 weeks for interface changes, longer for fundamental product changes.

The flip side also exists: a 'negative novelty effect' (sometimes called a 'novelty aversion' or 'change aversion') can cause initial disengagement with a new design that eventually recovers. Both cases argue for running experiments to steady state.

Option A's 'contamination' explanation is backwards: control users learning about the new design would increase control engagement (compressing the gap), but the data shows the treatment arm's engagement DECREASING while control is stable — consistent with novelty wearing off, not control contamination.

Option C is wrong: monotonic decline in an apparent treatment effect is a signal to investigate, not a sign the experiment is invalid.

Option D is false: digital interface experiments are particularly prone to novelty effects, especially for UI redesigns where new layouts and interactions trigger exploratory behavior.
hints: Why would users who saw a new interface be MORE engaged in week 1 than week 4, even if the interface change has no lasting value?
If the treatment arm engagement drops by 14pp over 4 weeks while the control stays flat, what does that suggest about the source of the week-1 lift?

title: Minimum Detectable Effect for an A/B Test
description:
Implement `solve(n_per_arm, sigma, alpha=0.05, power=0.80)` that computes the **minimum detectable effect (MDE)** — the smallest absolute difference in means that a two-sample z-test can detect with the given parameters.

Formula: MDE = (z_{α/2} + z_{β}) × σ × √(2/n)

Use `statistics.NormalDist` for z-score lookup. Return a float.
solution_code:
def solve(n_per_arm: int, sigma: float, alpha: float = 0.05, power: float = 0.80) -> float:
    import math
    from statistics import NormalDist
    # z_alpha2: upper critical value for two-sided test
    # z_beta:   power requirement (prob of detecting a true effect)
    z_alpha2 = NormalDist().inv_cdf(1 - alpha / 2)   # ≈ 1.96 for α=0.05
    z_beta = NormalDist().inv_cdf(power)              # ≈ 0.84 for 80% power
    return (z_alpha2 + z_beta) * sigma * math.sqrt(2 / n_per_arm)
explanation: MDE = (z_{α/2} + z_β) × σ × √(2/n). For α=0.05, power=0.80: z_{α/2} ≈ 1.96, z_β ≈ 0.84. The √(2/n) factor comes from the standard error of the difference in two equal-sized groups: SE = σ√(1/n + 1/n) = σ√(2/n). Larger n or smaller σ → smaller MDE (more sensitive experiment). This formula assumes equal arms, known σ, and normally distributed outcomes.
hints: The MDE formula uses two z-scores: one for the significance threshold (z_{α/2}) and one for the power requirement (z_β). `statistics.NormalDist().inv_cdf(p)` gives the z-score such that P(Z ≤ z) = p.
The standard error of the difference between two equal-sized groups is σ × √(2/n), not σ/√n.

title: What Does a 95% Confidence Interval Actually Claim?
description:
Your team ran 500 visitors through a landing page. 35 converted (7% conversion rate). A frequentist analysis yields a 95% confidence interval of [4.9%, 9.3%] for the true conversion rate.

The PM says: 'So we're 95% confident the true rate is somewhere in that range, right?'

Which of the following most accurately explains what the interval means?
options: Yes — it means there is a 95% probability that the true conversion rate falls between 4.9% and 9.3% given this data

The interval is a frequentist construct: if we repeated this experiment under identical conditions many times and computed an interval each time, 95% of those intervals would contain the true (fixed, unknown) conversion rate. This specific interval either contains the true rate or it doesn't — frequentist inference doesn't assign a probability to a fixed parameter
The 95% refers to the confidence in the statistical software, not in the result itself
It means we are 95% sure the sample estimate of 7% is unbiased and therefore within 5% of the true value
explanation:
Option B is the technically correct frequentist interpretation. In the frequentist framework, the conversion rate is a fixed (though unknown) constant — it either is or isn't between 4.9% and 9.3%. Probability statements about fixed constants are not meaningful in frequentist statistics.

The 95% refers to the long-run coverage rate of the procedure: if you ran many experiments with 500 users each and computed a 95% CI for each, approximately 95% of those intervals would cover the true conversion rate. The statement 'there is a 95% probability the true rate is in this interval' smuggles in a Bayesian interpretation (treating the parameter as a random variable), which is not what the frequentist CI computes.

Option A is the most common misinterpretation — and the intuitive one. It is what a Bayesian credible interval would say (given a suitable prior), but NOT what a frequentist CI claims.

Options C and D are wrong. C is not a statistical concept. D confuses the confidence level with a bound on bias, which are unrelated concepts.

This distinction matters in practice: when a PM asks 'are we confident the rate is above 5%?', the CI [4.9%, 9.3%] does not directly answer that question — it requires a Bayesian credible interval with an explicit prior to make that statement.
hints: In the frequentist framework, the true conversion rate is a fixed number — not a random variable. What kind of probability statement can you make about a fixed constant?
The 95% in '95% CI' refers to a property of the procedure used to build the interval, not a property of this specific interval.

title: Bayesian Credible Interval: What Claim Does It Make?
description:
Continuing from the landing page experiment (35/500 conversions). A Bayesian analyst uses a Beta(1, 1) prior — encoding no prior knowledge about the conversion rate — and observes 35 successes from 500 trials.

The Bayesian posterior is Beta(36, 466), and the 95% highest-density interval (credible interval) is approximately [5.0%, 9.4%].

The PM asks: 'This range is almost the same as the frequentist CI. So they mean the same thing, right?'

Which response is most accurate?
options: Yes — when the prior is uniform and the sample is large, the two intervals converge numerically and conceptually

The intervals are numerically similar here, but they mean different things. The Bayesian credible interval directly answers: 'Given the data and the uniform prior, there is a 95% probability the true conversion rate lies between 5.0% and 9.4%.' The frequentist CI cannot make this statement. The conceptual difference is real even when the numbers agree
The Bayesian interval is always wider than the frequentist CI because it accounts for prior uncertainty
The two intervals are unrelated; the Bayesian result is only valid if the prior is informed by historical data
explanation:
Option B is correct. The numerical similarity is a well-known result (related to the Bernstein-von Mises theorem), but the conceptual difference is fundamental.

The Bayesian credible interval is a statement about the posterior distribution of the parameter: it says 'given this data and this prior, there is a 95% posterior probability that θ lies in this interval.' This is exactly the statement the PM intuitively wanted from the frequentist CI — and it is now valid to make, because in the Bayesian framework θ is treated as a random variable with a probability distribution.

The frequentist CI [4.9%, 9.3%] means 'this procedure, if repeated many times, would produce intervals covering the true θ 95% of the time.' It does NOT mean 'P(θ ∈ [4.9%, 9.3%] | data) = 0.95.'

Key insight: the conceptual choice between frameworks determines what question you're answering. With a uniform prior and 500 data points, the answers happen to be numerically close. But with a small sample (say n = 20) or an informative prior, the two intervals would diverge both numerically and conceptually.

Option A is wrong because the conceptual difference persists even when the numbers converge. Numerical agreement doesn't make the interpretations equivalent.

Option C is wrong — there is no general rule that Bayesian intervals are wider. With an informative prior that concentrates mass near the true value, Bayesian intervals can be narrower.

Option D is wrong: using a uniform prior with observational data is a valid choice. It encodes 'I have no prior information' — a reasonable starting point when no historical data exists.
hints: In one statistical framework, a parameter is a fixed unknown constant; in the other, it is a random variable with a distribution. Which framework allows direct probability statements about where the parameter lies?
The PM wanted to say 'the true rate is 95% likely to be in this range.' Which framework lets you make that exact statement, and what does it require?

title: As Sample Size Grows: Bayesian and Frequentist Convergence
description:
The product team reruns the landing page experiment at 10× scale — 5,000 visitors, 350 conversions (still 7%). The Bayesian analyst uses the same Beta(1, 1) prior.

At n = 500: frequentist 95% CI ≈ [4.9%, 9.3%], Bayesian 95% CI ≈ [5.0%, 9.4%] — nearly identical.
At n = 5,000: what happens to the relationship between the two intervals?
options: The two intervals diverge as n grows because the Bayesian interval carries the weight of the prior, which becomes more influential at large sample sizes

Both intervals narrow substantially (inversely with √n), and they remain very close to each other numerically. With large n, the data overwhelm any reasonable prior — the likelihood dominates the posterior, and the Bayesian and frequentist intervals are asymptotically equivalent. The 95% CI and credible interval interpret differently but point to the same range
The frequentist interval narrows with √n but the Bayesian interval stays constant because the Beta(1,1) prior fixes the credible interval width
At n = 5,000, the frequentist interval is invalid because the normal approximation breaks down at large sample sizes
explanation:
Option B correctly describes the asymptotic behaviour. Both intervals narrow in proportion to 1/√n: with 5,000 observations instead of 500, the standard error of the proportion drops by √10 ≈ 3.16×, so both intervals would be roughly 3× narrower — approximately [6.3%, 7.7%] for both.

The Bernstein-von Mises theorem formalises this: under mild regularity conditions, as n → ∞ the posterior distribution concentrates around the maximum likelihood estimate, and the Bayesian credible interval and frequentist confidence interval converge to the same numerical range. The conceptual interpretation remains different (posterior probability vs. coverage frequency), but the practical difference in the numbers vanishes.

The intuition: with 5,000 data points, the Beta(1,1) prior (which contains the equivalent weight of 2 observations) becomes negligible compared to the 5,000 observations. The data overwhelm the prior.

Option A inverts the role of the prior: more data means the data dominate, not the prior. A prior is most influential at small sample sizes.

Option C is wrong: the Bayesian interval narrows with n just as the frequentist CI does. The posterior is updated by every additional observation; it doesn't stay fixed.

Option D is wrong: the normal approximation becomes MORE accurate at large sample sizes, not less. The CLT guarantees that the sampling distribution of the proportion converges to normal as n increases.
hints: As n increases, which term in the posterior Beta(alpha_prior + successes, beta_prior + failures) dominates — the prior parameters or the data?
Think about what happens to the width of any 95% interval as the standard error shrinks. Do both frameworks use the same variance in their formulas?

title: Prior Strength: How Quickly Does Data Overcome a Prior?
description:
Two analysts model the same experiment — 50 conversions out of 200 visits (25% rate):

- Analyst A uses a Beta(1, 1) prior (uniform, no prior knowledge)
- Analyst B uses a Beta(40, 160) prior (encoding strong prior belief that conversion is ~20%)

Both compute the posterior distribution.

Analyst B's posterior mean is 22.5%, while Analyst A's posterior mean is 25.1%. The PM says 'Analyst A is right — your data shows 25%, so Analyst B must be wrong to put it at 22.5%.'

What is the most accurate characterisation of what is happening?
options: The PM is right: with 200 observations, the data should completely override any prior. Analyst B's prior is introducing bias

Both analysts are applying Bayes' rule correctly. Analyst B's prior is equivalent to having seen 200 additional observations with a 20% rate; it takes substantial data to overcome. With only 200 new observations and a strong prior encoding 200 pseudo-observations, the posterior is pulled toward the midpoint between prior and data. Neither posterior is 'biased' — they represent different prior states of knowledge
Analyst A's posterior is correct and Analyst B's prior is invalid because it encodes a specific numerical belief without empirical evidence
Analyst B should use a Jeffreys prior instead of Beta(40,160) to avoid subjectivity
explanation:
Option B is correct. The Beta(40, 160) prior is equivalent in effective sample size to 200 pseudo-observations encoding a 20% conversion rate. When Analyst B then observes 200 real observations (50 successes), the posterior is:

Beta(40 + 50, 160 + 150) = Beta(90, 310)

Posterior mean = 90 / (90 + 310) = 90/400 = 22.5%

This is effectively the weighted average of the prior belief (20%) and the data (25%), with equal weight given to the prior (200 pseudo-obs) and the data (200 real obs). With a strong prior, 200 data points is not enough to overwhelm it — you'd need something like 2,000 observations for the data to dominate a Beta(40,160) prior.

The PM's claim that 'the data should completely override the prior' treats the prior as arbitrary noise. But a prior represents accumulated domain knowledge. Analyst B may have good reasons for their prior (e.g., the company's historical conversion rate across 100 past campaigns is stably around 20%). Ignoring that information is not 'more objective' — it's discarding valid evidence.

Option A frames the prior as 'bias,' which misunderstands the Bayesian framework. Prior information is a feature, not a bug — it encodes what you knew before the experiment.

Option C is wrong for the same reason: a prior backed by domain knowledge or historical data is entirely valid. 'Empirical evidence' can include prior campaigns, expert knowledge, or physical constraints on the parameter.

Option D: Jeffreys priors are used when you want an 'objective' prior that is invariant under reparameterisation; they are not the only valid choice, and the question of which prior to use depends on the context.
hints: The Beta(40,160) prior is equivalent in information content to having previously observed how many successes and failures? Compare that to the 200 new observations.
The posterior mean for a Beta-Binomial update is a weighted average of the prior mean and the data proportion. What are the weights?

title: Beta-Binomial Posterior Update
description:
Implement `solve(alpha_prior, beta_prior, successes, trials)` that returns the tuple `(alpha_posterior, beta_posterior)` after updating a Beta prior with binomial observations.

For a Beta(α, β) prior with k successes from n trials, the posterior is Beta(α + k, β + n − k).
expected_code:
def solve(alpha_prior: float, beta_prior: float, successes: int, trials: int) -> tuple[float, float]:
    return (alpha_prior + successes, beta_prior + trials - successes)
solution_code:
def solve(alpha_prior: float, beta_prior: float, successes: int, trials: int) -> tuple[float, float]:
    # Beta-Binomial conjugate update:
    # Prior:    Beta(alpha, beta)
    # Likelihood: Binomial(n, theta), k successes
    # Posterior: Beta(alpha + k, beta + n - k)
    alpha_post = alpha_prior + successes
    beta_post = beta_prior + trials - successes
    return (alpha_post, beta_post)
explanation: The Beta distribution is the conjugate prior for the Binomial likelihood. Conjugacy means the posterior is in the same family as the prior, making the update closed-form: the α parameter (encoding successes) gains the observed successes, and the β parameter (encoding failures) gains the observed failures. Posterior mean = α_post / (α_post + β_post). The Beta parameters have a 'pseudo-count' interpretation: α represents prior successes, β prior failures.
hints: The Beta distribution's two parameters encode prior counts of successes (α) and failures (β). Observing k more successes and n−k more failures adds directly to each count.
Write out the posterior parameters as algebraic expressions of alpha_prior, beta_prior, k, and n. The conjugate update formula is a single addition for each parameter.

title: Confidence Interval for a Conversion Rate
description:
A product runs 500 landing page visits, observing 35 conversions (7%). A data scientist computes a 95% Wald confidence interval:

p̂ ± z_{0.025} × √(p̂(1−p̂)/n) = [4.8%, 9.2%]

The PM says: 'The lower bound is under 5%, which is our minimum viable threshold. We shouldn't launch.'

A statistician responds: 'That interpretation is too strong — this is not what the CI tells you to do.'

Who is closer to correct, and why?
options: The PM is correct: if the CI lower bound is below the threshold, the data are consistent with a failure scenario and the product should not launch

The statistician is closer to correct. The CI width reflects uncertainty about the true rate — not a decision criterion. A proper launch decision requires pre-specifying what evidence level would trigger launch vs. hold, and ideally a one-sided test against the 5% threshold. The CI lower bound being below 5% means the data is 'consistent with' rates below 5%, but that's not the same as saying the true rate is probably below 5%
Both are wrong: a CI cannot be used to make launch decisions; only Bayesian inference can answer this question
The PM's reasoning is valid: any CI that includes values below the threshold means the experiment failed to demonstrate viability
explanation:
Option B is correct. Using the CI lower bound as a hard decision threshold is a common but imprecise approach to decision-making.

The 95% CI [4.8%, 9.2%] says: the procedure generating this interval would capture the true rate 95% of the time. It does NOT say 'the true rate is 95% likely to be in this range' (that's Bayesian), and it does NOT say 'the true rate is probably below 5%.' The point estimate is 7%, which is above 5%.

For a rigorous launch decision against a minimum viable threshold, the correct approach is a one-sided hypothesis test: H₀: p ≤ 0.05 vs. H₁: p > 0.05, pre-specified before the experiment. If p = 0.07 with n = 500, the one-sided p-value against H₀: p = 0.05 is p ≈ 0.03 — evidence for exceeding the threshold. The CI lower bound is not a direct answer to 'is the rate above 5%?'

Option A treats the CI lower bound as a probability statement about the parameter — a Bayesian interpretation applied to a frequentist tool.

Option C is too strong: CIs can inform decisions, but the decision rule needs to be appropriate. The issue is not that CIs can't help — it's that the PM is applying an overly conservative decision rule (lower bound must exceed threshold) rather than a calibrated one.

Option D repeats the PM's error: a CI 'being consistent with' values below a threshold is a statement about coverage, not about the probability the true value is below that threshold.
hints: The point estimate is 7%, which is above the 5% threshold. The CI lower bound being below 5% is a statement about uncertainty. What would you need to directly test whether the true rate exceeds 5%?
For a one-sided launch decision ('is the rate above X?'), which statistical test is more directly applicable than reading the CI lower bound?

title: Data Quality: When Is the Wald CI Unreliable?
description:
Continuing from the conversion rate study (35/500, 7%). The data scientist used the Wald CI: p̂ ± z × √(p̂(1−p̂)/n) = [4.8%, 9.2%].

A colleague mentions: 'The Wald CI performs poorly in some common situations. When should you use a different CI method for proportions?'

The data scientist asks: 'What cases break the Wald CI?'

Which best characterises when the Wald CI is unreliable for proportions?
options: The Wald CI is always reliable for n > 30, regardless of the proportion; the Central Limit Theorem guarantees accuracy

The Wald CI is unreliable when p̂ is near 0 or 1 (rare events or near-certain events), when n is small (say n < 50), or when the expected cell counts np̂ or n(1−p̂) fall below ~5. In these cases, the normal approximation to the Binomial is poor and the Wald CI has poor coverage — it nominally claims 95% but actually covers the true rate only 80–90% of the time. Wilson or Clopper-Pearson intervals are better alternatives
The Wald CI is unreliable only when the sample is not drawn randomly; any non-random sample invalidates it
The Wald CI always undercovers; the correct CI for proportions is always the Bayesian credible interval
explanation:
Option B correctly identifies the well-known failure modes of the Wald CI for proportions.

The Wald CI applies a normal approximation: p̂ ≈ N(p, p(1−p)/n). This approximation is valid when both np̂ and n(1−p̂) are reasonably large (rule of thumb: each ≥ 5 or 10). When p̂ is close to 0 or 1, or when n is small, the Binomial distribution is asymmetric and the normal approximation fails.

Consequences of Wald CI failure:
- The interval can extend below 0 or above 1 (physically impossible)
- Coverage probability oscillates and can fall well below the nominal 95%
- For p̂ close to 0, the CI is often too narrow (overconfident)

In our example (p̂ = 0.07, n = 500): np̂ = 35 ≥ 10, n(1−p̂) = 465 ≥ 10 — the Wald CI is adequate here. But if we had 7 conversions from 100 visits (same rate, smaller n), or 2 conversions from 500 (very rare event), the Wald CI would be unreliable.

Better alternatives:
- Wilson interval: better coverage near boundaries, doesn't go below 0
- Clopper-Pearson: exact interval (conservative, guaranteed coverage)
- Agresti-Coull ('add 2 successes and 2 failures'): simple approximation with better coverage

Option A is wrong: the CLT requires both np̂ and n(1−p̂) to be large, not just n > 30. A sample of n = 1,000 with p̂ = 0.001 still violates the approximation.

Option C is wrong: the approximation concern is about the distributional assumption, not the sampling method.

Option D is wrong: the Wald CI is adequate in most moderate-sample, moderate-proportion settings. The Bayesian CI is an alternative framework, not a universal replacement.
hints: The Wald CI uses a normal approximation to the Binomial. Under what conditions is the Binomial well-approximated by a Normal? What happens at the extremes (p near 0 or 1)?
What are the minimum expected cell counts (np̂ and n(1−p̂)) often cited as the rule of thumb for when the normal approximation is adequate?

title: Bootstrap CI vs Parametric CI: When to Bootstrap
description:
A data scientist computes the 95% confidence interval for **median** session duration from 200 observations. Session duration is highly right-skewed (most sessions are short; a few are very long).

Option A: Parametric CI using mean ± z × σ/√n  
Option B: Bootstrap percentile CI with 2,000 resamples

The analyst uses Option A. A colleague argues Option B is better here. Who is right and why?
options: Option A is always correct when n ≥ 30 because the CLT guarantees the sampling distribution of any statistic is normal

Option B (bootstrap) is better here for two reasons: (1) the target statistic is the **median**, not the mean — the CLT applies to the mean but not automatically to other statistics; (2) session duration is highly skewed, so the normal approximation may be poor for small/moderate samples. The bootstrap makes no distributional assumption and directly estimates the sampling distribution of the median empirically
Both intervals are equivalent; the CLT makes Option A exact for any sample size above 30
Option A is better because bootstrapping introduces randomness that reduces the validity of the CI
explanation:
Option B correctly identifies why bootstrapping is preferable here.

The CLT guarantees that the sampling distribution of the **sample mean** converges to a normal distribution as n increases, regardless of the population distribution. It does NOT guarantee this for the median, variance, or other statistics — though in practice the CLT applies to many smooth estimators via the delta method.

For the median specifically: the sampling distribution of the sample median is approximately normal for large n (it has its own CLT), but the variance formula requires knowledge of the population density at the median, which is unknown. The bootstrap avoids this entirely by empirically estimating the sampling distribution.

For highly right-skewed distributions (like session duration), the normal approximation for any statistic can be poor at n = 200 — the skewness in the population propagates to the sampling distribution. Bootstrapping makes no normality assumption; it estimates the sampling distribution by resampling from the data itself.

Bootstrap limitation: the bootstrap assumes the sample is representative of the population. With n = 200 from a skewed distribution, the tails may be underrepresented, which can lead to bootstrap CIs that undercover the extreme quantiles. But this is a second-order concern compared to the misspecification in Option A.

Option A's error is applying a mean-specific formula (mean ± z × σ/√n) to the median. These are different estimators with different sampling distributions.

Option C repeats the common CLT misapplication — the CLT is for the mean, not 'any statistic.'

Option D is wrong: bootstrap randomness is controlled by seed and reduces as n_resamples increases. The bootstrap is a valid statistical procedure with well-established coverage properties.
hints: The CLT says the sampling distribution of the *mean* is asymptotically normal. Is the target statistic here the mean or the median? Does the CLT apply directly?
For a heavily right-skewed metric, what assumption does the parametric CI (mean ± z × SE) make about the sampling distribution? Is that assumption likely to hold with n = 200?

title: Bootstrap CI Width and Resample Count Trade-off
description:
Continuing from the bootstrap CI analysis: the analyst runs two versions of the bootstrap for the same dataset:
- Version 1: 200 resamples → 95% CI: [42s, 118s]
- Version 2: 5,000 resamples → 95% CI: [44s, 112s]

A PM asks: 'Why does the CI change slightly between 200 and 5,000 resamples? And should we always use 5,000?'

Which response is most accurate?
options: The CI changes because more resamples always produce a narrower (more accurate) CI, so you should always use the maximum resamples computationally feasible

The CI changes because 200 resamples is insufficient to estimate the percentiles of the bootstrap distribution stably — there's Monte Carlo variance in the percentile estimates. With 5,000 resamples, the 2.5th and 97.5th percentile estimates stabilize. However, more resamples do NOT narrow the CI itself; they reduce the Monte Carlo noise in estimating the CI endpoints. The CI width reflects sampling variability in the original data, not the number of resamples
The CI narrows because more resamples mean more data, which reduces statistical uncertainty
200 resamples is statistically sufficient for any bootstrap CI; the width change is due to numerical precision differences, not Monte Carlo variance
explanation:
Option B correctly distinguishes two sources of variation: (1) Monte Carlo noise from insufficient resamples, and (2) true sampling uncertainty from the original data.

A bootstrap CI estimates the sampling distribution of the median by resampling from the observed data. With only 200 resamples, the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the bootstrap distribution are estimated from just 5 and 195 values respectively — highly variable. With 5,000 resamples, those percentiles are estimated from 125 and 4,875 values — much more stable.

Critically: the CI width reflects the variability of the median in the original sample of n = 200 observations. Adding more resamples does not add more information about the population — it only reduces Monte Carlo noise in reading the bootstrap percentiles. If the underlying data showed high variation in session duration, the CI would be wide regardless of whether you use 200 or 50,000 resamples.

Rule of thumb: 2,000 resamples is usually sufficient for percentile CIs; 10,000 for higher precision or BCa (bias-corrected accelerated) intervals.

Option A confuses reducing Monte Carlo noise with reducing the CI itself. More resamples reduce the imprecision in estimating the CI endpoints, but the CI width is ultimately determined by the data, not the number of resamples.

Option C makes the same error — 'more resamples = more data' is wrong. The bootstrap always resamples from the same n original observations.

Option D is too dismissive: 200 resamples often produces visibly unstable percentile estimates, especially in the tails. 2,000+ is the practical minimum.
hints: The bootstrap uses the original n observations over and over. Does adding more resamples add new observations from the population, or does it just repeat sampling from the same n data points?

Two sources of variation: (a) sampling variability in the original data (drives CI width), and (b) Monte Carlo noise from finite resamples (drives instability in CI endpoints). Which one does increasing resamples address?

title: Bootstrap CI Reliability at Very Small and Very Large n
description:
The analyst now considers using the same bootstrap percentile CI in two new contexts:

- **Context A:** n = 15 observations of session duration (very small)
- **Context B:** n = 100,000 observations of session duration (very large)

For which context is the bootstrap percentile CI most reliable, and what is the key concern in each?
options: Context A: the bootstrap is more reliable at small n because it makes no distributional assumptions, which is especially valuable when normality can't be verified

Context B is more reliable. At small n (Context A), the bootstrap CI can be unreliable because the bootstrap assumes the sample is a good approximation of the population — with n = 15 from a right-skewed distribution, extreme values in the tail are likely underrepresented or absent. This causes the bootstrap distribution to underestimate tail uncertainty and produce CIs that undercover. At large n (Context B), the sample more fully represents the population and the bootstrap is reliable; the main concern is computational cost
Neither is reliable; the bootstrap requires n ≥ 1,000 to give valid CIs
Both are equally reliable; the bootstrap has perfect coverage guarantees regardless of sample size
explanation:
Option B correctly identifies the direction of reliability and the key failure mode at small n.

The bootstrap CI relies on the fundamental assumption that the sample is a sufficiently representative approximation of the population distribution. With n = 15 from a right-skewed distribution:
- The maximum observed value is likely far below the true distribution maximum
- The tail of the distribution — which drives CI width for skewed metrics — is sparsely or not represented in the 15 observations
- Bootstrap resamples cannot 'invent' extreme values that didn't appear in the original sample
- Result: the bootstrap CI is likely too narrow (undercoverage), underestimating the true uncertainty

At n = 100,000:
- The sample covers the distribution densely, including tails
- The bootstrap assumption is well-satisfied
- The CI is computationally expensive (100,000 rows × 5,000 resamples = 500M values), but valid
- Computational mitigation: subsample to ~10,000 before bootstrapping if needed

Option A inverts the reliability direction. The distribution-free assumption is indeed an advantage, but it doesn't rescue the bootstrap from the fundamental problem that small samples can't represent rare events in the population tails.

Option C is too conservative — the bootstrap works reasonably well for n ≥ 50–100 in moderate-skewness settings, but n = 15 is genuinely risky for skewed distributions.

Option D is wrong: bootstrap coverage properties depend on sample size and distributional assumptions. Perfect coverage is never guaranteed.
hints: At n = 15 from a right-skewed distribution, how well represented are the extreme high values in the sample? Can the bootstrap generate them if they weren't in the original 15 observations?
What is the bootstrap's core assumption about the relationship between the sample and the population? Under what sample size conditions does that assumption hold well?

title: Failed to Reject ≠ No Effect: Diagnosing a Type II Risk
description:
A product team tests a redesigned onboarding flow with n = 500 users per arm. Baseline conversion: 10%. Expected conversion for the new flow: 15% (5pp lift).

The result: p = 0.09 (not significant at α = 0.05). The team concludes: 'No effect — the redesign doesn't work.'

A statistician says: 'You may have committed a Type II error. This conclusion is premature.'

Why might the statistician be right?
options: The statistician is wrong: p = 0.09 proves the null is true, so the conclusion is correct

A Type II error is failing to reject a false null hypothesis (missing a real effect). With only 500 users per arm and a 5pp effect size, the experiment may be underpowered — there is a meaningful probability of getting p > 0.05 even if the 5pp lift is real. The experiment cannot distinguish 'no effect' from 'effect too small to detect at this sample size'
Type II errors only occur when α > 0.05; at α = 0.05 there are no Type II errors
Type II errors are impossible in randomised experiments; only observational studies can commit them
explanation:
Option B is correct. A Type II error (false negative, missed effect) occurs when a real effect exists but the test fails to reach the significance threshold. The probability of a Type II error is 1 − power.

With n = 500 per arm, baseline p₁ = 10%, and true effect p₂ = 15%, the power of a two-sided two-proportion z-test is approximately 67%. This means there is roughly a 33% chance of getting p > 0.05 even if the 5pp lift is real. The team has a significant risk of a Type II error.

The correct interpretation of p = 0.09 is: 'We found insufficient evidence to conclude the new flow is better at this sample size and significance level.' This is very different from 'the new flow has no effect.'

The experiment can distinguish between two scenarios: (a) there truly is no effect, and (b) there is a real effect of ~5pp but the experiment was underpowered to detect it. Without computing power, you cannot know which scenario is more likely.

Option A is the fundamental misinterpretation of hypothesis testing: failing to reject the null does not prove the null is true.

Option C is wrong: α = 0.05 determines the Type I error rate (false positives), not the presence or absence of Type II errors.

Option D is wrong: Type II errors are properties of any hypothesis test, randomised or observational. Randomisation eliminates confounding but does not affect the power of the test.
hints: Type II error = failing to reject a false null. What would the power of this test be if the true effect really is 5pp? Would 500 users per arm be enough?
What are the two explanations for p = 0.09? (a) No effect, or (b) ______. How do you distinguish between them?

title: Computing Power for a Two-Proportion Z-Test
description:
Implement `solve(n_per_arm, p1, p2, alpha=0.05)` that computes the **statistical power** of a two-sided two-proportion z-test.

Approach:
1. Compute the standard error under the alternative: `se_alt = sqrt(p1*(1−p1)/n + p2*(1−p2)/n)`
2. Compute the non-centrality parameter: `ncp = |p2 − p1| / se_alt`
3. Power = Φ(ncp − z_{α/2}) + Φ(−ncp − z_{α/2})

Use `statistics.NormalDist` for both z-score lookup and CDF. Return a float rounded to 4 decimal places.
expected_code:
def solve(n_per_arm: int, p1: float, p2: float, alpha: float = 0.05) -> float:
    import math
    from statistics import NormalDist
    z_c = NormalDist().inv_cdf(1 - alpha / 2)
    se_alt = math.sqrt(p1 * (1 - p1) / n_per_arm + p2 * (1 - p2) / n_per_arm)
    ncp = abs(p2 - p1) / se_alt
    power = NormalDist().cdf(ncp - z_c) + NormalDist().cdf(-ncp - z_c)
    return round(power, 4)
solution_code:
def solve(n_per_arm: int, p1: float, p2: float, alpha: float = 0.05) -> float:
    import math
    from statistics import NormalDist
    z_c = NormalDist().inv_cdf(1 - alpha / 2)  # critical z for two-sided test
    # SE under the alternative hypothesis
    se_alt = math.sqrt(p1 * (1 - p1) / n_per_arm + p2 * (1 - p2) / n_per_arm)
    # Non-centrality: how many SEs the true effect is from zero
    ncp = abs(p2 - p1) / se_alt
    # Power = P(reject | true effect)
    # Two-sided: Phi(ncp - z_c) + Phi(-ncp - z_c) [second term ~0 for reasonable ncp]
    power = NormalDist().cdf(ncp - z_c) + NormalDist().cdf(-ncp - z_c)
    return round(power, 4)
explanation: Power is the probability of correctly rejecting H₀ when the alternative H₁ is true. For the two-proportion case, the non-centrality parameter ncp = |p2−p1| / SE_alt measures how many standard errors the true effect is from zero. Power = Φ(ncp − z_c) for the upper tail, plus the negligible lower tail. Larger n → larger ncp → higher power. Smaller effect → smaller ncp → lower power.
hints: Power uses the standard error under the *alternative* hypothesis, not under the null. Under H₁, the true proportions are p1 and p2, so SE_alt = sqrt(p1*(1-p1)/n + p2*(1-p2)/n).
The non-centrality parameter ncp = |p2 - p1| / SE_alt tells you how many SEs the true effect is from zero. Power ≈ Phi(ncp - z_critical).

title: Statistically Significant but Practically Meaningless
description:
The team scales the onboarding experiment to n = 50,000 per arm. Result: conversion increases from 10.0% to 10.2% (0.2pp lift), p = 0.003.

The PM declares: 'Highly significant! Ship it.'

A data scientist says: 'Wait — significance doesn't mean the effect is worth shipping.'

Who is right, and what should happen next?
options: The PM is right: p = 0.003 is well below any reasonable threshold, so the effect is both statistically and practically meaningful

The data scientist is right. With 50,000 users per arm, the test has extremely high power — it can detect even tiny effects. A 0.2pp lift may be statistically significant but practically negligible (e.g., if the feature adds user friction, costs engineering resources, or the lift is too small to justify opportunity cost). Statistical significance answers 'is the effect reliably non-zero?' — not 'is the effect big enough to matter?'
Neither: a p-value of 0.003 means the effect size is 0.3pp, not 0.2pp
The data scientist is wrong: in large-scale product experiments, statistical significance always implies practical significance
explanation:
Option B correctly identifies the disconnect between statistical and practical significance at large sample sizes.

With n = 50,000 per arm, the experiment has enormous power — it can detect effects as small as 0.1pp with >80% power. At this scale, virtually any non-zero effect becomes statistically significant. A 0.2pp lift from 10.0% to 10.2% may be:

- Real and reliably detected (the p-value is valid)
- Practically insignificant — if the feature requires ongoing engineering maintenance, adds a step to the flow, increases load time, or has downstream effects on other metrics

This is sometimes called the 'curse of large samples': when n is large enough, even negligibly small effects reach significance. The solution is to pre-specify a **minimum practical effect size** (minimum business-relevant lift) before the experiment — and judge results against that threshold, not just p < 0.05.

For this product decision, the team should ask: 'Is a 0.2pp conversion lift worth the cost and risk of shipping this feature?' That is a business question, not a statistical one.

Option A conflates statistical significance with practical importance — the core error. p = 0.003 answers 'how reliably has this non-zero effect been estimated?' It does not answer 'is this effect worth acting on?'

Option C is wrong: the p-value is not a measure of effect size. It is the probability of observing data at least this extreme under the null.

Option D is wrong: this is the exact misconception the question is designed to refute. In large-scale experimentation, statistical significance and practical significance diverge widely.
hints: With 50,000 users per arm, what is the minimum detectable effect at 80% power? Can you distinguish 'statistically significant' from 'practically significant'?
Before running the experiment, what threshold of conversion lift would justify shipping this feature? Is 0.2pp above or below that threshold?

title: Optional Stopping: Peeking Inflates Type I Error
description:
An analyst runs an A/B test and checks the results daily. On Day 1 (n = 50/arm): p = 0.38. Day 3: p = 0.12. Day 8: p = 0.04. The analyst stops the experiment and reports: 'Significant at p = 0.04 after 8 days.'

A statistician says the Type I error rate for this decision is much higher than 5%.

What is the correct explanation?
options: There is no problem: p = 0.04 is p = 0.04 regardless of when you look

Optional stopping inflates Type I error. Each daily check is an implicit hypothesis test. With 8 tests at α = 0.05, the probability of spuriously hitting p < 0.05 at least once under the null is approximately 1 − (0.95)⁸ ≈ 34%. The analyst has not truly run a single 5% test — they've run a sequential procedure without adjusting the stopping rule or the significance threshold, which inflates the false positive rate far beyond 5%
The Type I error rate is unaffected by peeking as long as the final decision uses p < 0.05
The p = 0.04 on Day 8 is invalid because the sample size keeps changing; a fixed sample size is required for any p-value to be valid
explanation:
Option B correctly identifies the optional stopping problem, also called 'peeking' or 'data dredging.'

Each time the analyst looks at the p-value and considers stopping, they are implicitly running a hypothesis test. Under the null hypothesis (no effect), the p-value follows a uniform distribution — but the minimum of K uniform [0,1] values is systematically below any threshold. The more times you look, the higher the probability that the p-value dips below 0.05 at some point by chance.

With 8 independent checks at α = 0.05 each, the family-wise Type I error rate is approximately 1 − (1 − 0.05)⁸ ≈ 34% (this is an upper bound, as checks are not truly independent — the p-value on day 8 is correlated with day 7). More rigorous sequential analysis shows the actual inflation is somewhat less but still substantial.

Solutions:
- **Pre-specify the sample size** before running, and look only once at the end
- **Sequential probability ratio test (SPRT)** or always-valid confidence sequences: statistical methods designed for continuous monitoring that control error rates at every look
- **Group sequential methods** (e.g., O'Brien-Fleming): pre-specified interim looks with adjusted significance thresholds at each look

Option A is the intuitive but incorrect belief: p = 0.04 computed after 8 looks does not have the same interpretation as p = 0.04 from a pre-planned single analysis.

Option C is wrong and restates Option A's error.

Option D is incorrect: a single pre-planned analysis with a fixed sample size is what's needed, not a changing n per se. The p-value on day 8 uses a specific n — the problem is the multiple looks, not the sample size changing.
hints: If you flip a fair coin and check after each flip, how likely are you to see 3 heads in a row at some point over 10 flips? How does that compare to checking only after 10 flips?
Each time the analyst checks and doesn't stop, they're implicitly running a test. How does running 8 tests at α=0.05 affect the overall false positive rate?

title: Absence of Evidence Is Not Evidence of Absence
description:
A team powers an experiment to detect a 2pp conversion lift with 80% power. The experiment runs to full sample size. Result: +0.8pp, p = 0.31 (not significant).

A stakeholder says: 'We proved the feature has no effect. Let's kill it.'

What is the correct statistical response?
options: The stakeholder is correct: a non-significant result proves the null hypothesis is true

The experiment was powered only for effects ≥ 2pp. A 0.8pp effect would likely not be detected at this sample size — the test has low power against the alternative of +0.8pp. The correct conclusion is: 'We found no evidence of an effect ≥ 2pp' — not 'there is no effect.' The feature may still have a real but smaller-than-expected effect below the detection threshold
Since p = 0.31 is larger than 0.05, it means there is a 31% chance the null is true
A larger sample would have given a smaller p-value, so the team should increase n and re-run without changing α
explanation:
Option B states the correct inference. This is the principle that 'absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.'

The experiment was designed with 80% power to detect a 2pp effect. This means:
- If the true effect is 2pp, there is an 80% chance of getting p < 0.05
- If the true effect is 0.8pp (much smaller), the power against this smaller alternative is substantially less than 80% — perhaps 20–30%
- Getting p = 0.31 with +0.8pp observed is entirely consistent with a real 0.8pp effect that this experiment was not designed to detect

The experiment can rule out effects ≥ 2pp (if the true effect were 2pp, we had 80% chance to detect it and didn't). It cannot rule out effects below 2pp.

For a more defensible conclusion that there's 'no meaningful effect,' the team would need to:
1. Pre-specify an equivalence margin (e.g., '±0.5pp is clinically/practically equivalent to zero')
2. Run an equivalence test or compute a confidence interval and check whether the CI falls entirely within the equivalence margin

Option A is the fundamental frequentist error: failing to reject H₀ does not imply H₀ is true.

Option C misinterprets the p-value as the probability the null is true. The p-value is P(data this extreme | H₀ is true) — not P(H₀ is true | data). These are different conditional probabilities.

Option D describes a form of optional stopping: increasing n and re-running after seeing p = 0.31 would inflate the Type I error rate if the same α = 0.05 threshold is used without correction.
hints: The experiment was powered to detect a 2pp effect. What is the power against a 0.8pp effect? Can you conclude from p=0.31 that effects smaller than 2pp don't exist?
What would you need to run to formally conclude 'the effect is practically zero'? (Hint: it's not a standard superiority test.)

title: Birthday Problem: Counter-Intuitive Collision Probability
description:
A company assigns each new user a random 4-digit PIN (0000–9999) at signup — 10,000 possible PINs. The security team says: 'With 200 users, the chance that any two users share a PIN is low — only 200/10,000 = 2%.'

A data scientist says the collision probability is actually much higher.

Who is correct, and what is the approximate probability that at least two users share the same PIN among 200 users?
options: The security team is correct: 200/10,000 = 2% is the correct collision probability

The data scientist is correct. This is analogous to the birthday problem: the probability that all 200 users have distinct PINs is approximately (10000/10000) × (9999/10000) × ... × (9801/10000) ≈ e^{−200×199/(2×10000)} ≈ e^{−1.99} ≈ 13.7%, so the collision probability is about 86%
The collision probability is 200²/10000 = 4% — the security team's calculation should be squared
The exact answer requires knowing the hash function used, not just the number of PINs
explanation:
Option B is correct. The security team's error is computing the probability that one specific user's PIN matches another user's (200/10000 × 1 = 2% if one fixed user checks against 200 others) rather than the probability that ANY pair collides.

For the birthday problem: P(all 200 PINs distinct) = ∏ₖ₌₀¹⁹⁹ (10000 − k)/10000 ≈ e^{−n(n-1)/(2N)} where n=200, N=10000. This gives e^{−200×199/20000} = e^{−1.99} ≈ 0.137.

So P(at least one collision) ≈ 1 − 0.137 = 86.3%. With 200 users and 10,000 PINs, there is an 86% chance two users share a PIN — far from the intuitive 2%.

The security team's calculation answers the wrong question: 'what fraction of PINs are taken?' not 'what is the probability of at least one collision?' The birthday paradox arises because the number of pairs grows quadratically: 200 users create 200×199/2 ≈ 19,900 pairs, and each pair has a 1/10,000 chance of matching.

This has direct security implications: with 4-digit PINs, an organisation of even moderate size faces near-certain PIN collisions, which can enable account-enumeration attacks.
